title: Designing for people
author: Visual Slides

slides.title: Designing for people
slides.subtitle: Understand the experience, then decide what to build.
slides.background_alt: Illustrative photo: a team placing sticky notes on a wall during a design sprint
slides.body_html:
Research, shared questions, sketches and feedback make an idea easier to understand and improve.

A practical view of the design process
slides.notes_en: Start with the person using a product or service. The design process helps us understand their situation, make a useful question clear, and try possible answers. The next slides show how to make that process visible.
slides.notes_zh: 先理解人 再决定做什么
slides.speaker: Presenter

slides.title: The whole experience
slides.subtitle: Consider what happens before, during and after someone uses the product.
slides.background_alt: Illustrative notes blending into a dark background
slides.body_html:
Look beyond the object

A useful feature is part of a larger journey. Someone must find it, understand it, use it and tell whether it worked.

What does this feel like for the person?

Listen to the situation behind the feedback. A score can show dissatisfaction; the story helps explain why it matters.
slides.notes_en: Consider the whole experience. A feature may exist, but can someone find it, understand it, use it and check the result? Listening to the situation behind the feedback helps us understand what matters to the person.
slides.speaker: Presenter

slides.title: From observation to a test
slides.subtitle: Connect what you saw to a question you can answer.
slides.background_alt: Illustrative grouped notes behind the framework
slides.body_html:
Start with a pause

If someone stops after saving, ask what signal would help them know the change went through.

Use what you learn

Show a simple confirmation. If the person still checks elsewhere, ask what gives them confidence and revisit the question.
slides.notes_en: Start with a specific task and watch where someone pauses. Describe the need as a question, then try one idea that can answer it. Go back to the question if the test reveals something you did not expect.
slides.notes_zh: 观察停顿 提问 尝试 再回看
slides.speaker: Presenter

backdrop.alt: Illustrative photo: a whiteboard covered in grouped notes

slides.title: Make the activity visible
slides.subtitle: Connect each visual to an activity, a learning question and an output.
slides.body_html:
Observe

Understand the situation

Use an actual interview or observation photograph when presenting real work. Explain what the team wanted to learn.

Make sense of it

Compare directions

Show the team sharing or grouping ideas. State how the discussion helped choose what to explore.

Decide what to test

Make a question tangible

A sketch gives people something to discuss and change before investing in a complete solution.
slides.source_credit: Illustrative diagrams. They do not document a real research project.
slides.notes_en: A process image needs an explanation. Say what people are doing, what they are trying to learn, and what decision follows. Use real project photographs for observation and workshops. These neutral illustrations show the layout, rather than claiming research evidence.
slides.notes_zh: 照片要说清活动 学习和决定
slides.speaker: Presenter

slides.title: Build enough to answer a question
slides.subtitle: Choose a prototype form that fits the learning question.
slides.body_html:
Rough sketch

Discuss the structure

A quick sketch helps reveal whether the arrangement makes sense while changes are inexpensive.

Several alternatives

Compare possible answers

Make different directions visible. Keep the same user need in view when choosing which to try.

Working prototype

Observe a realistic task

Build the interaction needed for the question. Watch where someone hesitates and ask what they expected.
slides.notes_en: Each prototype should answer a question. A rough sketch helps us discuss structure, alternatives help us compare directions, and a working prototype lets us observe a realistic task. More detail is useful only when the question needs it.
key_phrases: Each prototype should answer a question
slides.speaker: Presenter

slides.title: Keep learning in use
slides.subtitle: Use feedback to decide what to improve and whether to expand.
slides.body_html:
Try with a small group

See what people actually do

Use a limited trial to understand the experience in a realistic setting. Keep the research question visible.

Refine and decide

Check what changed

Combine observed behavior with feedback. A completed release does not by itself show that the original need has been met.

What should we understand before deciding what to build?
slides.notes_en: The learning continues when an idea reaches real use. Start with a suitable small group, understand what happens, then decide what to change or expand. Return to the main question: what should we understand before deciding what to build? The person and their problem.
slides.notes_zh: 把真实使用变成下一步的依据
slides.speaker: Presenter
